compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional interview planning session, either person could draw up a long guide or suggest another follow-up. The number of questions depends on the work and cannot distinguish the types.

Shared N and P help explain why both descriptions emphasise noticing possibilities and staying open to new information. Either person can write a short or a long guide, depending on what the research requires.

The difference sits on two axes. E/I asks where attention and energy go more often: other people and the room outside, or inner thinking and sorting. T/F asks which basis judgement takes first: a standard that applies consistently, or what this means for the people involved. The two axes must be read separately, and neither can be replaced by word count, speaking pace or the order in which a guide gets written.

### ENFP and INTP: two emphases in one guide — the hook and the definition

In this fictional research project, both people review the same interview guide, consent requirements and deliverable. One question is whether the wording respects participants’ circumstances. Another is whether a definition can be applied consistently across interviews. Either person can ask both.

Those questions illustrate two decision criteria relevant to T/F. To illustrate E/I, keep the research question fixed and consider whether working through it in conversation or in private reflection helps someone clarify it.

Training, the deliverable and the participant’s needs may determine what gets written first. The order cannot distinguish the types.

In comparable situations, it is more useful to ask what mattered in the choice. A single edit or reason cannot establish someone’s type.

### ENFP and INTP: why Ne and Si are shared while the dominant changes

In the type-dynamics model, E/I specifies the attitude of the dominant process. The shared P indicates an outward perceiving process, Ne in both descriptions. Ne is dominant for ENFP and auxiliary for INTP, whose dominant process is Ti. The judging functions also differ: Fi and Te in ENFP, Ti and Fe in INTP.

In this arrangement ENFP has Ne dominant, Fi second, Te third, Si last; INTP has Ti dominant, Ne second, Si third, Fe last. ENFP's second-seat Fi takes part in value trade-offs — whether this matches what I genuinely care about; it is not a synonym for being good with people, and not the same as being able to break the ice. The last seat does not mean rarely used, and does not mean it can only be called on at the end. The four positions are processing positions in the model, carrying no frequency or sequence; a process marked inferior may well be used first in some situations.

Sharing Ne and Si says only that both stacks contain these two perceiving processes, in different seats; it does not say the two draw on the same material, and does not say the processing order is the same. compare_blocks.body:
Boundary of use: the three scenes below are editorial fiction, used only to compare two possible trade-offs; they are not for dividing work and not for typing. Either type can do user research, and either can do interviewing, coding and write-up well; competence depends on training, experience and the requirements of the task.

One researcher may want to improve the guide while another wants to check how the records will be compared. Agree what the guide needs to accomplish and how you will judge the evidence. Either person can raise either issue.

### ENFP and INTP: designing a user-interview guide

(Fictional scene) The same task: eight new users, forty minutes each, finding out why something was installed and then not used, with a formatted record due in three days.

One approach writes the entry as a question that invites a story: not why don't you use it, but when did you last open it and what were you doing then; plus two softening sentences so the person does not feel interrogated. The other splits "not using it" into three situations — never used, used and stopped, switched to another product — and writes a decision rule for each, so the eight records can be compared afterwards.

Each has a cost. The first may dig out unexpected reasons, but the eight records may end up with entirely different themes, making it hard to say anything about prevalence; the second is more comparable but may turn the interviewee into an answer machine, and the real reason never surfaces. The cost has nothing to do with preference; it relates to research experience, deliverable requirements and the mix of interviewees.

A workable arrangement runs in two parts: a story-style entry first, branch-style follow-ups after, with the lengths adjusted to the interviewee's state. That is not a fixed recipe and does not map to a type; experienced researchers switch back and forth within one session. Stopping to compare notes after the third interviewee is only an example, not a threshold. The review looks at four things: whether the phrasing led the answer; whether the answer gave a specific experience bearing on the research question; whether similar answers came from independent mentions; and whether different answers might just be sample variation, since new users and long-standing users face different situations.

Speaking up more is a clue, not proof that the entry worked; one nod or one "more or less" cannot stand alone as evidence for a conclusion.

### ENFP and INTP: can this conclusion go into the report

(Fictional scene) Eight interviews done, three interviewees mention too many notifications, so they turned it off. One candidate sentence sits on the table: users generally find notifications excessive. Two reactions are both possible.

One leans toward writing it in: those three raised it unprompted, the words were specific, and it supports a detailed paragraph. The other leans toward narrowing: the questions were not identical and the sample is eight, so the most that can be written is that the phrasing appeared in this round; "generally" goes beyond the material.

In this fictional report review, an observation can be worth recording even when it cannot support a claim about users in general. Both researchers need to distinguish what was said from how far the conclusion can extend.

A workable approach records the number of mentions and the asking conditions. This round can be written as: three of eight interviewees raised excessive notifications unprompted; those three mentioned it under the following phrasings. The asking conditions have to be stated: whether it came from an open question, from a follow-up, or from a list of options. If neither can be written, put it under to be verified rather than in the main conclusion. No type thereby gets a lower evidential bar.

### ENFP and INTP: a cousin wants to drop out and learn programming

(Fictional scene) When a younger relative asks for direction, two lines of questioning are both possible. He is in his second year, wants to leave university for a bootcamp, and says he could be employed within six months.

One line asks about experience and motive first: have you written a line of code, have you asked anyone doing this work, what is it you actually want to leave. The other breaks the path and the conditions first: front end or back end, what the bootcamp teaches, what goes on the CV in six months, whether you could return to university afterwards.

Discussing the person’s reasons can clarify what they hope to change. Checking entry requirements, costs and realistic next steps tests whether an option is feasible. Either person can ask both sets of questions. Neither approach establishes a type or makes the decision for the student.

The check can be handed to him: write two lines — how many hours a week I can give over the next six months, and what I will have to show for it at the end — then read the bootcamp's contract and refund terms and talk to someone studying or working in the field. Both lines have to be in his hand; someone answering for him does not count. This kind of decision is not divided by type, and is not made by someone else on his behalf.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The most common thing taken as evidence is word count. Who talks more in an interview is often set by role — main interviewer, note-taker, observer — and by preparation and familiarity with the interviewee. Either type may only listen for a whole session, and either can talk for ten minutes about their own reasoning. Word count cannot prove E or I.

Either type can ask about someone’s circumstances, definitions or counterexamples. What is useful depends on the question and the evidence. A single follow-up cannot identify a type.

The third treats revising the guide as not having thought it through. There are many reasons to revise: on-site reaction, two questions turning out to repeat, running out of time, a change of deliverable format. The revision itself does not type anyone, and the reason has to be read across situations.

The fourth takes E for someone who should talk more and I for someone who does not express themselves. E/I describes where attention and energy go more often, not expressive ability and not willingness to socialise; either type may talk at length on a familiar subject, and either may listen first in an unfamiliar setting.

The fifth takes F for only tending feelings and T for disregarding people. F puts people and values into the weighing, which does not mean being unable to set a standard; T weighs a consistently applicable standard, which does not mean being unable to look after people.

body: When two results differ, check the item bank first: the same version, the same language, the same scoring definition; then whether you were referring to everyday preference or to the requirements of a particular post, project or course. body: In a fictional interview planning session, either person could draw up a long guide or suggest another follow-up. The number of questions depends on the work and cannot distinguish the types.

Shared N and P help explain why both descriptions emphasise noticing possibilities and staying open to new information. Either person can write a short or a long guide, depending on what the research requires.

The difference sits on two axes. E/I asks where attention and energy go more often: other people and the room outside, or inner thinking and sorting. T/F asks which basis judgement takes first: a standard that applies consistently, or what this means for the people involved. The two axes must be read separately, and neither can be replaced by word count, speaking pace or the order in which a guide gets written.
### ENFP and INTP: two emphases in one guide — the hook and the definition

In this fictional research project, both people review the same interview guide, consent requirements and deliverable. One question is whether the wording respects participants’ circumstances. Another is whether a definition can be applied consistently across interviews. Either person can ask both.

Those questions illustrate two decision criteria relevant to T/F. To illustrate E/I, keep the research question fixed and consider whether working through it in conversation or in private reflection helps someone clarify it.
Training, the deliverable and the participant’s needs may determine what gets written first. The order cannot distinguish the types.
In comparable situations, it is more useful to ask what mattered in the choice. A single edit or reason cannot establish someone’s type.
### ENFP and INTP: why Ne and Si are shared while the dominant changes

In the type-dynamics model, E/I specifies the attitude of the dominant process. The shared P indicates an outward perceiving process, Ne in both descriptions. Ne is dominant for ENFP and auxiliary for INTP, whose dominant process is Ti. The judging functions also differ: Fi and Te in ENFP, Ti and Fe in INTP.

In this arrangement ENFP has Ne dominant, Fi second, Te third, Si last; INTP has Ti dominant, Ne second, Si third, Fe last. ENFP's second-seat Fi takes part in value trade-offs — whether this matches what I genuinely care about; it is not a synonym for being good with people, and not the same as being able to break the ice. The last seat does not mean rarely used, and does not mean it can only be called on at the end. The four positions are processing positions in the model, carrying no frequency or sequence; a process marked inferior may well be used first in some situations.

Sharing Ne and Si says only that both stacks contain these two perceiving processes, in different seats; it does not say the two draw on the same material, and does not say the processing order is the same. The attitude of the third process (Te in ENFP, Si in INTP) is labelled differently elsewhere — check the source when versions differ, and do not use it as evidence. Base descriptions sit on the [ENFP profile](/en/personality/enfp) and the [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp).

body: Boundary of use: the three scenes below are editorial fiction, used only to compare two possible trade-offs; they are not for dividing work and not for typing. Either type can do user research, and either can do interviewing, coding and write-up well; competence depends on training, experience and the requirements of the task.

One researcher may want to improve the guide while another wants to check how the records will be compared. Agree what the guide needs to accomplish and how you will judge the evidence. Either person can raise either issue.
### ENFP and INTP: designing a user-interview guide
(Fictional scene) The same task: eight new users, forty minutes each, finding out why something was installed and then not used, with a formatted record due in three days.

One approach writes the entry as a question that invites a story: not why don't you use it, but when did you last open it and what were you doing then; plus two softening sentences so the person does not feel interrogated. The other splits "not using it" into three situations — never used, used and stopped, switched to another product — and writes a decision rule for each, so the eight records can be compared afterwards.

Each has a cost. The first may dig out unexpected reasons, but the eight records may end up with entirely different themes, making it hard to say anything about prevalence; the second is more comparable but may turn the interviewee into an answer machine, and the real reason never surfaces. The cost has nothing to do with preference; it relates to research experience, deliverable requirements and the mix of interviewees.

A workable arrangement runs in two parts: a story-style entry first, branch-style follow-ups after, with the lengths adjusted to the interviewee's state. That is not a fixed recipe and does not map to a type; experienced researchers switch back and forth within one session. Stopping to compare notes after the third interviewee is only an example, not a threshold. The review looks at four things: whether the phrasing led the answer; whether the answer gave a specific experience bearing on the research question; whether similar answers came from independent mentions; and whether different answers might just be sample variation, since new users and long-standing users face different situations.
Speaking up more is a clue, not proof that the entry worked; one nod or one "more or less" cannot stand alone as evidence for a conclusion.
### ENFP and INTP: can this conclusion go into the report

(Fictional scene) Eight interviews done, three interviewees mention too many notifications, so they turned it off. One candidate sentence sits on the table: users generally find notifications excessive. Two reactions are both possible.

One leans toward writing it in: those three raised it unprompted, the words were specific, and it supports a detailed paragraph. The other leans toward narrowing: the questions were not identical and the sample is eight, so the most that can be written is that the phrasing appeared in this round; "generally" goes beyond the material.

In this fictional report review, an observation can be worth recording even when it cannot support a claim about users in general. Both researchers need to distinguish what was said from how far the conclusion can extend.

A workable approach records the number of mentions and the asking conditions. This round can be written as: three of eight interviewees raised excessive notifications unprompted; those three mentioned it under the following phrasings. The asking conditions have to be stated: whether it came from an open question, from a follow-up, or from a list of options. If neither can be written, put it under to be verified rather than in the main conclusion. No type thereby gets a lower evidential bar.
### ENFP and INTP: a cousin wants to drop out and learn programming

(Fictional scene) When a younger relative asks for direction, two lines of questioning are both possible. He is in his second year, wants to leave university for a bootcamp, and says he could be employed within six months.

One line asks about experience and motive first: have you written a line of code, have you asked anyone doing this work, what is it you actually want to leave. The other breaks the path and the conditions first: front end or back end, what the bootcamp teaches, what goes on the CV in six months, whether you could return to university afterwards.

Discussing the person’s reasons can clarify what they hope to change. Checking entry requirements, costs and realistic next steps tests whether an option is feasible. Either person can ask both sets of questions. Neither approach establishes a type or makes the decision for the student.

The check can be handed to him: write two lines — how many hours a week I can give over the next six months, and what I will have to show for it at the end — then read the bootcamp's contract and refund terms and talk to someone studying or working in the field. Both lines have to be in his hand; someone answering for him does not count. This kind of decision is not divided by type, and is not made by someone else on his behalf.

body: The most common thing taken as evidence is word count. Who talks more in an interview is often set by role — main interviewer, note-taker, observer — and by preparation and familiarity with the interviewee. Either type may only listen for a whole session, and either can talk for ten minutes about their own reasoning. Word count cannot prove E or I.
Either type can ask about someone’s circumstances, definitions or counterexamples. What is useful depends on the question and the evidence. A single follow-up cannot identify a type.

The third treats revising the guide as not having thought it through. There are many reasons to revise: on-site reaction, two questions turning out to repeat, running out of time, a change of deliverable format. The revision itself does not type anyone, and the reason has to be read across situations.

The fourth takes E for someone who should talk more and I for someone who does not express themselves. E/I describes where attention and energy go more often, not expressive ability and not willingness to socialise; either type may talk at length on a familiar subject, and either may listen first in an unfamiliar setting.

The fifth takes F for only tending feelings and T for disregarding people. F puts people and values into the weighing, which does not mean being unable to set a standard; T weighs a consistently applicable standard, which does not mean being unable to look after people.

body: When two results differ, check the item bank first: the same version, the same language, the same scoring definition; then whether you were referring to everyday preference or to the requirements of a particular post, project or course. The latter is worth noting, but which side it pushes you toward has no fixed direction.

If the same tool puts both E/I and T/F near a boundary, that only means the classification was sensitive to differences in answering; there is no need to choose between two labels in a hurry, and it cannot be inferred that you switch freely between two approaches. Without dimension scores or scoring notes, do not infer a near-boundary result.

To keep observing, look at two things separately: whether attention and energy land more on the people and business in the room, or on your own thinking and sorting; and whether judgement more often asks whether a standard applies consistently, or what this means for the people involved. Those two questions correspond to E/I and T/F, and do not involve the order of actions.

The practice can sit inside the work: after several interviews in a row, write one sentence each time about which question you most want to change and why. If the reasons are mostly the person did not understand what I was asking, this question repeats the last one, there was not enough time, or it drifted from the research question, those are records of working habit, not typing rules, and no reason is assigned to a type.

They do not predict the order of actions, frequency of use or areas of strength, and they do not say who suits research or whether two people get along. On the same guide either type may write the definitions first, and either may think first about how to get the other person talking.
sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In a fictional interview planning session, either person could draw up a long guide or suggest another follow-up. The number of questions depends on the work and cannot distinguish the types.

Shared N and P help explain why both descriptions emphasise noticing possibilities and staying open to new information. Either person can write a short or a long guide, depending on what the research requires.

The difference sits on two axes. E/I asks where attention and energy go more often: other people and the room outside, or inner thinking and sorting. T/F asks which basis judgement takes first: a standard that applies consistently, or what this means for the people involved. The two axes must be read separately, and neither can be replaced by word count, speaking pace or the order in which a guide gets written.

### ENFP and INTP: two emphases in one guide — the hook and the definition

In this fictional research project, both people review the same interview guide, consent requirements and deliverable. One question is whether the wording respects participants’ circumstances. Another is whether a definition can be applied consistently across interviews. Either person can ask both.

Those questions illustrate two decision criteria relevant to T/F. To illustrate E/I, keep the research question fixed and consider whether working through it in conversation or in private reflection helps someone clarify it.

Training, the deliverable and the participant’s needs may determine what gets written first. The order cannot distinguish the types.

In comparable situations, it is more useful to ask what mattered in the choice. A single edit or reason cannot establish someone’s type.

### ENFP and INTP: why Ne and Si are shared while the dominant changes

In the type-dynamics model, E/I specifies the attitude of the dominant process. The shared P indicates an outward perceiving process, Ne in both descriptions. Ne is dominant for ENFP and auxiliary for INTP, whose dominant process is Ti. The judging functions also differ: Fi and Te in ENFP, Ti and Fe in INTP.

In this arrangement ENFP has Ne dominant, Fi second, Te third, Si last; INTP has Ti dominant, Ne second, Si third, Fe last. ENFP's second-seat Fi takes part in value trade-offs — whether this matches what I genuinely care about; it is not a synonym for being good with people, and not the same as being able to break the ice. The last seat does not mean rarely used, and does not mean it can only be called on at the end. The four positions are processing positions in the model, carrying no frequency or sequence; a process marked inferior may well be used first in some situations.

Sharing Ne and Si says only that both stacks contain these two perceiving processes, in different seats; it does not say the two draw on the same material, and does not say the processing order is the same. The attitude of the third process (Te in ENFP, Si in INTP) is labelled differently elsewhere — check the source when versions differ, and do not use it as evidence. Base descriptions sit on the [ENFP profile](/en/personality/enfp) and the [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp).

sections.body_md:
This comparison fixes the conditions: the same eight interviewees, the same question about why something was installed and then not used, forty minutes each, all recorded, conclusions due in three days. Change the conditions and both columns change: if one is the main interviewer and the other only observing, role will swamp preference; if the interviewees are long-standing users, the entry to the question has to change too.

Either type can use both approaches. The table compares possible emphases under the same conditions. The consent and evidence requirements apply to everyone.

| Shared task | ENFP: possible emphasis | INTP: possible emphasis | Preference illustrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Both choose between the same opening questions | Which wording respects the participant’s comfort and circumstances | Which wording applies the same definition of non-use across interviews | T/F · Decision criteria |
| Both consider the same follow-up after hearing a participant’s answer | Whether it accounts for what the participant told them about their situation | Whether it uses the same criteria as comparable follow-ups | T/F · Decision criteria |
| Both review the same interview guide | Clarify how it works by discussing it with the team | Clarify how it works by reflecting on it privately | E/I · Direction of attention |
| Both consider the same draft conclusion and verified transcripts | Whether the wording represents the participants and their circumstances fairly | Whether the interpretation applies the same criteria to all comparable records | T/F · Decision criteria |
| Both consider whether to continue after a participant becomes upset | What continuing would mean for the participant in this situation | How the agreed criteria for pausing apply to this situation | T/F · Decision criteria. Both follow the same consent and safety requirements. |
| Both hear the same unexpected answer | Notice possible explanations the team had overlooked | Notice possible explanations the team had overlooked | Shared N · This cannot distinguish the types |

The same person can use both sets of considerations. Training, assigned duties and the participant’s needs shape the work. These rows cannot measure skill or identify a type.
sections.title: ENFP and INTP in one minute

sections.body_md:
Boundary of use: the three scenes below are editorial fiction, used only to compare two possible trade-offs; they are not for dividing work and not for typing. Either type can do user research, and either can do interviewing, coding and write-up well; competence depends on training, experience and the requirements of the task.

One researcher may want to improve the guide while another wants to check how the records will be compared. Agree what the guide needs to accomplish and how you will judge the evidence. Either person can raise either issue.

### ENFP and INTP: designing a user-interview guide

(Fictional scene) The same task: eight new users, forty minutes each, finding out why something was installed and then not used, with a formatted record due in three days.

One approach writes the entry as a question that invites a story: not why don't you use it, but when did you last open it and what were you doing then; plus two softening sentences so the person does not feel interrogated. The other splits "not using it" into three situations — never used, used and stopped, switched to another product — and writes a decision rule for each, so the eight records can be compared afterwards.

Each has a cost. The first may dig out unexpected reasons, but the eight records may end up with entirely different themes, making it hard to say anything about prevalence; the second is more comparable but may turn the interviewee into an answer machine, and the real reason never surfaces. The cost has nothing to do with preference; it relates to research experience, deliverable requirements and the mix of interviewees.

A workable arrangement runs in two parts: a story-style entry first, branch-style follow-ups after, with the lengths adjusted to the interviewee's state. That is not a fixed recipe and does not map to a type; experienced researchers switch back and forth within one session. Stopping to compare notes after the third interviewee is only an example, not a threshold. The review looks at four things: whether the phrasing led the answer; whether the answer gave a specific experience bearing on the research question; whether similar answers came from independent mentions; and whether different answers might just be sample variation, since new users and long-standing users face different situations.

Speaking up more is a clue, not proof that the entry worked; one nod or one "more or less" cannot stand alone as evidence for a conclusion.

### ENFP and INTP: can this conclusion go into the report

(Fictional scene) Eight interviews done, three interviewees mention too many notifications, so they turned it off. One candidate sentence sits on the table: users generally find notifications excessive. Two reactions are both possible.

One leans toward writing it in: those three raised it unprompted, the words were specific, and it supports a detailed paragraph. The other leans toward narrowing: the questions were not identical and the sample is eight, so the most that can be written is that the phrasing appeared in this round; "generally" goes beyond the material.

In this fictional report review, an observation can be worth recording even when it cannot support a claim about users in general. Both researchers need to distinguish what was said from how far the conclusion can extend.

A workable approach records the number of mentions and the asking conditions. This round can be written as: three of eight interviewees raised excessive notifications unprompted; those three mentioned it under the following phrasings. The asking conditions have to be stated: whether it came from an open question, from a follow-up, or from a list of options. If neither can be written, put it under to be verified rather than in the main conclusion. No type thereby gets a lower evidential bar.

### ENFP and INTP: a cousin wants to drop out and learn programming

(Fictional scene) When a younger relative asks for direction, two lines of questioning are both possible. He is in his second year, wants to leave university for a bootcamp, and says he could be employed within six months.

One line asks about experience and motive first: have you written a line of code, have you asked anyone doing this work, what is it you actually want to leave. The other breaks the path and the conditions first: front end or back end, what the bootcamp teaches, what goes on the CV in six months, whether you could return to university afterwards.

Discussing the person’s reasons can clarify what they hope to change. Checking entry requirements, costs and realistic next steps tests whether an option is feasible. Either person can ask both sets of questions. Neither approach establishes a type or makes the decision for the student.

The check can be handed to him: write two lines — how many hours a week I can give over the next six months, and what I will have to show for it at the end — then read the bootcamp's contract and refund terms and talk to someone studying or working in the field. Both lines have to be in his hand; someone answering for him does not count. This kind of decision is not divided by type, and is not made by someone else on his behalf.
sections.title: ENFP and INTP at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
The most common thing taken as evidence is word count. Who talks more in an interview is often set by role — main interviewer, note-taker, observer — and by preparation and familiarity with the interviewee. Either type may only listen for a whole session, and either can talk for ten minutes about their own reasoning. Word count cannot prove E or I.

Either type can ask about someone’s circumstances, definitions or counterexamples. What is useful depends on the question and the evidence. A single follow-up cannot identify a type.

The third treats revising the guide as not having thought it through. There are many reasons to revise: on-site reaction, two questions turning out to repeat, running out of time, a change of deliverable format. The revision itself does not type anyone, and the reason has to be read across situations.

The fourth takes E for someone who should talk more and I for someone who does not express themselves. E/I describes where attention and energy go more often, not expressive ability and not willingness to socialise; either type may talk at length on a familiar subject, and either may listen first in an unfamiliar setting.

The fifth takes F for only tending feelings and T for disregarding people. F puts people and values into the weighing, which does not mean being unable to set a standard; T weighs a consistently applicable standard, which does not mean being unable to look after people.
sections.title: ENFP and INTP: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check the item bank first: the same version, the same language, the same scoring definition; then whether you were referring to everyday preference or to the requirements of a particular post, project or course. The latter is worth noting, but which side it pushes you toward has no fixed direction.

If the same tool puts both E/I and T/F near a boundary, that only means the classification was sensitive to differences in answering; there is no need to choose between two labels in a hurry, and it cannot be inferred that you switch freely between two approaches. Without dimension scores or scoring notes, do not infer a near-boundary result.

To keep observing, look at two things separately: whether attention and energy land more on the people and business in the room, or on your own thinking and sorting; and whether judgement more often asks whether a standard applies consistently, or what this means for the people involved. Those two questions correspond to E/I and T/F, and do not involve the order of actions.

The practice can sit inside the work: after several interviews in a row, write one sentence each time about which question you most want to change and why. If the reasons are mostly the person did not understand what I was asking, this question repeats the last one, there was not enough time, or it drifted from the research question, those are records of working habit, not typing rules, and no reason is assigned to a type.
sections.title: ENFP and INTP: how to keep observing

items.answer:
There is no fixed point where ENFP and INTP stop understanding each other. Clarify whether you are discussing what happened, what it meant to the person or what conclusion the evidence supports.

They share Intuition and Perceiving and differ on E/I and T/F. One question is how someone makes sense of information, through interaction or private reflection. Another is what criteria they use to weigh a choice. Either person can ask about someone’s experience or check whether an account is consistent.
items.question: In conversation, where do they stop being on the same channel?

items.answer:
They share Ne and Si in this notation, but those processes occupy different positions. ENFP’s dominant process is Ne, and INTP’s is Ti.

In the four-function notation used here, ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si and INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe: Ne dominant and Si last in ENFP; Ti dominant, Ne auxiliary and Si third in INTP. Sharing two perceiving processes says only that both arrangements contain them, not that the material comes from the same place, and not that the processing order is the same. Position does not predict behaviour order or areas of strength, and does not say whether two people collaborate well or who attracts whom. Sources write the third process differently; check the source when versions differ.
items.question: They share two functions — why do they still read as two different people?

items.answer:
Yes. Both can care about a participant’s experience and write clear definitions. Function positions do not establish how often someone will do either.

What is worth watching is the reason, not whether it happens: across comparable situations, do you more often cite whether this standard applies consistently, or what this means for the people involved. A single performance or one phrase cannot assign a type.
items.question: An INTP also looks after an interviewee's feelings, an ENFP also pins down definitions?

items.answer:
Either. Competence depends on training, experience, task requirements and team configuration, not on four letters.

Interviewing includes defining the question, writing the guide, probing on the spot, coding and writing up; either type can do each stage, and people of both do them well. The division follows individual experience, interest in the task and project needs, not type. To learn about your own preference, take the same fictional records and have one person write both a story line and a coding table, and compare which you would rather produce and which skills you want to keep building; that result is for self-understanding, not for inferring a type.
items.question: Which is better suited to user research or interviewing?

items.answer:
A research team can disagree about when a claim is ready for the report. Check what each person thinks the evidence supports before deciding how to word it.

A workable agreement sets a deadline for each kind of work: the guide is finalised only on what to ask, and the coding rules can be settled later. In an argument, do one concrete thing first — write the candidate conclusion, have each mark the material supporting it and the gaps, then decide whether it goes into the main conclusion or under to be verified. That works better than arguing about whose standard is higher, and does not assign either side to a type.
items.question: Where do they jam when doing research together?

items.answer:
Check whether it was the same item set, the same language version and the same scoring definition, then whether both E/I and T/F sit near a boundary.

Near a boundary only means those two labels are sensitive to differences in answering; it cannot be inferred that you switch easily, and it does not mean two complete types both hold. Note the scene each sitting referred to: everyday preference, or the requirements of a post or project. For self-observation, look separately at the direction of attention and energy, and at which standard judgement values more, rather than at the order or number of actions in an interview.
items.question: Results keep moving between ENFP and INTP — which score do I look at first?

sections.body_md:
Preference definitions follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

The arrangement of the four positions on this page, in particular the attitude of the third process (Te in ENFP, Si in INTP), follows a common writing adopted here as an editorial convention; other sources handle it differently, and this page does not present the writing as the Foundation's only reading, nor imply that the Foundation's own tables use exactly this notation.

The three scenes — designing the interview guide, the scope of the report conclusion, and the cousin wanting to leave university for programming — are all editorial fiction, used to show possible trade-offs, not as evidence of type behaviour, and corresponding to no real person or event.

Assessment results are not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships, and type is not used to divide work within a team. Decisions about leaving university, training contracts or loans follow the contract terms and professional advice; clinical judgement belongs to qualified professionals.

The FermatMind assessment uses its own item bank and scoring, described in the [scoring and evidence note](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).
